summary: The day after Democrats won the US Congress, Canada waits for Thursday's budget, the Bank of Canada explains its rate hike, and Ontario keeps an OSAP audit secret.
body: Democrats won control of both the US Senate and House in Tuesday's midterms, and Canada's trade fight was on the ballot in places[^1]. In Maine, which buys about $4.1 billion a year from Canada, Democrat Troy Jackson beat Senator Susan Collins after a race that featured tariffs; in Michigan, the Republican candidate distanced himself from Trump's tariffs[^2][^1]. Prime Minister Mark Carney says talks with Washington are "more intense" but "we haven't finished"[^2].

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tables the federal budget on Thursday. He says it is about "regaining our ability to build", aiming for $1 trillion in private investment over five years, helped by a business tax deduction expected to cost about $36 billion over five years[^4]. His other priorities: new trade partners, Canadian industry, much higher defence spending and affordability[^5]. On Tuesday, Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem told MPs the bank raised its key rate to 2.5%, its first increase since July 2023, as war-driven oil prices push inflation to near 3%[^6]. He said government spending and fighting inflation are not "at odds"[^7].

For students: Ontario's Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn will not publish the KPMG audit of OSAP student aid at private career colleges, citing confidentiality; its early findings went to the OPP[^8]. The PC majority on a legislature committee voted down a Liberal motion for an auditor general probe, and NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government is trying "to sweep things under the carpet"[^8]. The schools in court filings deny wrongdoing[^8]. The province also told Toronto, which faces a $1.1-billion shortfall in 2027, that more money is not coming "right now"[^9].
differences: Analysts disagree on whether a Democratic Congress helps Canada. Asa McKercher says Congress could "reassert its control" over tariffs and strengthen Canada's hand, though Trump might "lash out"; Nicolas Schmitt says Canada "should not count on" a quick fix[^3].
